passage: The queue at the university admin office snaked into the corridor, rain dripping off umbrellas, and the scholarship deadline was at five. When Sabina finally reached the counter, the clerk didn't look up. 'Roll number.' She gave it. 'Out-of-state, na? Your lot always come with missing papers. Next!' He pushed her file back without reading it. Sabina stood in the corridor holding the damp file, feeling like a problem that had walked in by mistake. She had been in the city eight months, and the clerk had never once said her name. Then Bhupen from her lab saw her and came over. 'Sabina, what happened?' Hearing her own name, she almost cried. He read the slip: one page was missing a stamp. 'The hostel office has that stamp. Come, we'll run.' They got back at 4:52. Bhupen stayed in the queue with her.

qa.q: At what time did Sabina and Bhupen get back to the admin office?
qa.a: They got back at 4:52.

qa.q: Why did Sabina almost cry when Bhupen said her name?
qa.a: After eight months of being a roll number and treated as a problem, hearing her own name made her feel seen as a person again.

qa.q: What did Bhupen do that helped, beyond the stamp?
qa.a: Bhupen used Sabina's name, read the slip with her and stayed in the queue, so she wasn't facing the system alone as a number.

qa.q: How might things change if the clerk read each file and used names?
qa.a: The clerk might find fixable details instead of 'problems', and students like Sabina would leave feeling respected instead of like a burden.

grounding: Shows a student from another state treated by a clerk as a roll number and a burden, and a lab friend who calls her by name and stays with her.

passage: In the Laxmi Nagar PG, the owner called everyone by room numbers. Rukmini was 'Four'. 'Four, your mess money.' 'Four, don't use so much water, you people bathe twice a day.' When the power bill went up, the owner told a new tenant, 'It's these outside students, a burden on the whole building.' Rukmini had stopped answering at the door. She ate her curd rice on the bed, facing the wall, and on Sundays she spoke to no one at all. Then Aparna, from her statistics class, invited her home for lunch. Aparna's grandmother asked about Madurai, about the temple, about her amma's sambar. Rukmini talked for an hour. On the metro back she noticed she was humming. That night she video-called her cousin, then Aparna, and for the first time in weeks she slept straight through.

qa.q: What did the PG owner call Rukmini?
qa.a: The owner called Rukmini 'Four'.

qa.q: What does eating while facing the wall suggest about how Rukmini feels?
qa.a: It suggests Rukmini feels unseen and hurt, pulling away from people because being treated as a number and a burden has made her feel less than a person.

qa.q: What helped Rukmini begin to feel like herself again?
qa.a: Being welcomed at Aparna's home and asked about Madurai and her amma's sambar reconnected her with people who saw her, and she reached out to her cousin too.

qa.q: What might Aparna's grandmother have noticed during lunch?
qa.a: The grandmother may have noticed a quiet girl lighting up while talking about home, and enjoyed giving her a place to be herself.

grounding: Shows a student from another state called by a room number and treated as a burden, who is helped by people who ask about her life.

passage:
'Avni? You've gone quiet.'
'Sorry, di. Just tired.'
'You said that yesterday too. What's happening there?'
'Nothing. It's just... in lab, Sir calls me "Patna" instead of my name. Or "you, that one". Yesterday he said, "People like you fill our seats and then struggle." The whole class heard.'
Kashish was silent on the line. 'How long has this been going on?'
'Since August. I've stopped asking questions in lab. I feel like I'm just a seat.'
'Avni, you're not a seat. You're the girl who fixed Papa's inverter at twelve. And none of this is your fault.'
Avni laughed, wetly. 'That was once.'
'Listen. Call me every night this week. And right now, tonight, we'll write to your class mentor together, with dates and his exact words.'
'Okay.'
'And say your name when you ask a question. Loudly.'
'Avni,' she said, trying it out. 'Avni Kumari.'

qa.q: What does Sir call Avni instead of her name?
qa.a: Sir calls her 'Patna' or 'you, that one'.

qa.q: What does 'I feel like I'm just a seat' reveal about Avni?
qa.a: It reveals how being treated as a label has made Avni feel less than a person, enough to stop asking questions in lab.

qa.q: What did Kashish do that helped most?
qa.a: Kashish reminded Avni who she is with a real memory, said it wasn't her fault, kept her connected with nightly calls, and helped her write to the class mentor that same night.

qa.q: What might Kashish have felt during the silence on the line?
qa.a: Kashish was probably shocked and angry on her sister's behalf, and worried about how long Avni had carried it alone.

grounding: Shows a student from another state called by her city's name and treated as a seat-filler, and an elder sister who restores her name and helps her report it.

passage:
In my first winter in Dublin, I was a number more often than a name. At the immigration office I was 'fifty-eight'. At the accommodation desk I was 'another non-EU one', said to a colleague as if I couldn't hear. A tutor once sighed that international students 'take up all the help'. I started keeping my coat on in seminars, as if I might be asked to leave.
What pulled me back was small. My lab partner Thomas said 'Morning, Noor' every single day, and asked what I thought about the results before he wrote anything down. On Sundays I called my cousin in Lucknow, who laughed at all my stories.
I still flinch when I hear 'fifty-eight'. But I learned to spend more of my time with the people who say my name.

qa.q: What number was Noor called at the immigration office?
qa.a: Fifty-eight.

qa.q: What does keeping a coat on in seminars suggest about how Noor felt?
qa.a: It suggests Noor felt unwelcome and temporary, like a burden who might be asked to leave, rather than a student who belonged.

qa.q: What choice helped Noor through that winter?
qa.a: Noor chose to spend more time with people who used Noor's name, Thomas in the lab and the cousin on Sunday calls; those ties pushed back against feeling like a number.

qa.q: How might Thomas's daily 'Morning, Noor' have looked from Thomas's side?
qa.a: For Thomas it was probably ordinary politeness and teamwork, asking a partner's view first; he may not have known how much it meant to someone treated as a number elsewhere.

grounding: A migrant student called by a number and treated as a burden describes the hurt and how staying close to people who use their name helped.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Wednesday. Reena.
Joseph, second-year B.Com, from Aizawl, came in after the fee office sent him back a third time. The clerk calls him '4127' and told him in front of the queue, 'You outside students are always a headache.' He said the mess manager does the same: 'Next plate, next plate,' never a name.
He spoke quietly, looking at the floor. 'At home everyone knows me. Here I'm a roll number that causes trouble.' He has stopped going to evening football.
I used his name while we talked, and asked about home. He smiled for the first time when he described his mother's shop.
Next steps: I walked with him to the fee office and spoke to the clerk myself. He agreed to try football again on Friday; his classmate Lalrin plays there. Follow-up next Wednesday.

qa.q: What number does the fee clerk call Joseph?
qa.a: The clerk calls him '4127'.

qa.q: How does Joseph feel about being called a number, and what shows it?
qa.a: He feels unseen and like a burden; he speaks quietly, looks at the floor and says he is 'a roll number that causes trouble' here, though everyone knows him at home.

qa.q: Which of Reena's choices is most likely to help Joseph over time, and why?
qa.a: Encouraging him back to Friday football with his classmate Lalrin; staying connected to people who know his name will help more than one good meeting.

qa.q: How might the fee clerk's view of Joseph change after Reena came to the office with him?
qa.a: The clerk may start to see a student with a name rather than a file number, since being spoken to face to face makes it harder to call him a headache.

grounding: A counsellor records how a migrant student called by a roll number and a burden feels, and helps him reconnect with people who see him.

passage: Bhavna, you say nobody at your new college even knows your name. I understand that more than you think. Let your Shalini Aunty tell you. When I came from Thrissur to Delhi for my B.Sc., the hostel office called me 'Room 32' for the whole first term, and the mess manager called me 'extra plate'. One girl in my corridor said, loud enough for me to hear, that people like me were taking seats from local students. I stopped speaking at dinner. I felt like furniture delivered to the wrong address. What saved me was small. I wrote to my mother every Sunday, and she wrote back using every pet name she had for me. And the librarian, Mrs Arora, learnt my name in the second week and asked every morning if I'd eaten. Two people, Bhavna. Keep hold of the ones who say your name.

qa.q: What did the mess manager call Shalini?
qa.a: The mess manager called her 'extra plate'.

qa.q: How did being called 'Room 32' make Shalini feel?
qa.a: She felt hurt and unseen, like furniture delivered to the wrong address, and stopped speaking at dinner.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Shalini?
qa.a: Holding on to people who saw her: her mother's weekly letters and Mrs Arora learning her name and checking that she had eaten.

qa.q: How might Mrs Arora have seen the new student?
qa.a: Mrs Arora saw a young person far from home, not a room number, and chose to learn her name and look after her.

grounding: An aunt recalls being treated as a room number and a burden as a student from another state, and how people who used her name kept her going.

passage: The rain had been falling since noon, and Lokesh had lost his college ID somewhere between the bus stop and the library. At the hostel gate, the guard held up a hand. 'ID.' 'I lost it. I'm Lokesh, Room 214, second year—' 'No ID, no entry. You outside-state types are always losing things.' Water ran down Lokesh's neck. Two local students walked past and were waved through without being asked. He felt like a sack left out in the rain: counted, not seen. He stood under the dripping tin roof for twenty minutes, too tired to argue, phone at three percent. Then Tanuja from his lab ran up with her umbrella. 'Bhaiya, this is Lokesh. He's in my chemistry lab, he fixed our burner last week,' she told the guard, and called the warden on speaker. The warden said his name too, and the gate opened. That night Lokesh texted Tanuja: thank you for saying my name.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh feel 'like a sack left out in the rain'?

qa.q: What helped Lokesh get through the moment?
qa.a: Tanuja vouched for him by name, described him as a person, and called the warden, which reconnected him with people who saw him.

passage:
The Pune hostel office had a queue down the stairs. When Ishita reached the counter, the clerk didn't look up.
“Roll?”
“Forty-seven. I'm Ishita Chanu, from Imphal. My mess card isn't...”
“Forty-seven, north-east quota. You people always have card problems.” He slid a form across. “Next.”
It was the third time that week. The accounts section called her “the Imphal case.” The PT sir called her “Chinky” once, then laughed like it was nothing.
She walked back holding the form, feeling strangely thin, as if she were fading around the edges.
At the gate, Jahnavi, her lab partner, waved hard. “Ishita! Where were you? We saved you a plate of poha. Come, sit.”
Ishita sat. Jahnavi talked about the practical, asked about her mother's cold, said her name three more times without noticing.
Ishita felt herself come back, slowly.

qa.q: What number did the clerk use for Ishita?
qa.a: The clerk used her roll number, forty-seven, and called her “north-east quota.”

qa.q: How did Ishita feel walking back from the office?
qa.a: She felt hurt and invisible, “strangely thin” as if fading, because she kept being treated as a number or a case.

qa.q: How could a friend support someone treated like this?
qa.a: Like Jahnavi, by using their name, saving them a place and asking about their life, and by helping them report the slur to the college.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi see Ishita compared with the office staff?
qa.a: Jahnavi sees a friend with a name and a mother with a cold, not a roll number or quota.

grounding: The passage shows a migrant student being treated as a number and a problem, and being steadied by a friend who addresses her by name.

“Uma? You've gone quiet.” Ganga, her cousin, sounded tinny on speaker.
“Sorry. Long day.”
“What happened?”
“Nothing. The landlord came to collect rent. He talked to my roommate the whole time. About me. ‘These Bihar students, always late, always a headache.’ I was standing right there.”
“Did he say your name?”
“He doesn't know it. I'm ‘the Bihar one’. At the bank today, same. The man said, ‘You people, go to the other counter.’”
“Uma.”
“I just feel like a burden everywhere, Ganga-di. Like a problem on legs.”
“Listen. You are Uma, who made the top score in our district. Who fixes Nani's phone every holiday. Say it.”
Uma half laughed, half cried. “I'm Uma.”
“Good. Now tell me about your college friends. Who knows your name there?”
“Farzana. And Joel.”
“Call them tomorrow. Eat with them. Stay with people who see you.”

qa.q: What did the landlord call Uma?
qa.a: He called her “the Bihar one” and talked about “these Bihar students” as a headache.

qa.q: How does Uma feel after the landlord and the bank?
qa.a: She feels like a burden and invisible, “a problem on legs,” because nobody addresses her by name.

qa.q: What did Ganga advise, and why might it help?
qa.a: To spend time with Farzana and Joel, people who know her name; staying connected to people who see her helps her feel human again.

qa.q: If you were Ganga, hearing Uma go quiet, what would you want?
qa.a: Ganga would want Uma to feel remembered and not alone, which is why she reminds her of who she is.

grounding: The dialogue shows a migrant student treated as a burden and not addressed by name, and the comfort of staying connected to someone who sees her.

passage:
My first month in Delhi, I learned that I had several new names.
At the admissions desk I was “Nepal,” as in, “Nepal, sit there.” The flat owner wrote “Nepali girl” on the rent receipt instead of Binita Gurung. In the seminar, a professor once said, “Students like you cost the department,” and I spent the whole period staring at my notebook, feeling like a mistake.
I started going small. Eating late so the kitchen was empty. Not raising my hand.
It was Noor who noticed. She sat next to me in the library one evening and said, “Binita, you haven't told me one story about home. Tell me about Pokhara.” So I did. The lake, my father's tea stall, the dog that follows everyone.
We still meet every Thursday. When the world forgets my name, I know one person who never does.

qa.q: What did the flat owner write on the rent receipt?
qa.a: The flat owner wrote “Nepali girl” instead of Binita Gurung.

qa.q: How did Binita feel during the seminar comment, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and unwanted, staring at her notebook “feeling like a mistake” after being described as a cost.

qa.q: What helped Binita, and what could the college do too?
qa.a: Noor's regular, personal attention helped; the college could also make sure staff address students by name and take complaints about such remarks seriously.

qa.q: How does Noor see Binita?
qa.a: Noor sees her as a person with stories and a home in Pokhara, not as “Nepal” or a cost.

grounding: The first-person account shows a migrant student treated as a number or burden and the steadying effect of a friend who uses her name.

Hostel warden's note, first-year boys' hostel, by Farhan
Sahil came from a village in Bihar in July for engineering. Today he told me something I should have noticed. In the admin office, the clerk calls him "forty-seven", his roll number, never his name. In the mess, a senior told him, "You people come here and eat our seats." In class, when he asks a question, someone mutters, "Here comes the burden." He said, very quietly, "Sometimes I feel I'm not a person here. Just a number." He has stopped going to the canteen.
I told him plainly that what's happening is wrong and that he belongs here as much as anyone.
What I did next: I spoke to the admin clerk and the mess senior this afternoon. I also introduced Sahil to Rakesh, a second-year from his district, and asked the two of them to have dinner together tonight. I'll meet Sahil again on Friday.

qa.a: The clerk calls him "forty-seven", his roll number, never his name.

qa.q: How does Sahil feel about being treated this way?
qa.a: Sahil feels deeply hurt and invisible, as if he is not a person, just a number.

qa.q: What did Farhan do that could help Sahil stay connected?
qa.a: Farhan spoke to the clerk and senior that same afternoon and introduced Sahil to Rakesh from his district for dinner.

qa.q: How might Rakesh see Sahil at dinner?
qa.a: Rakesh would likely see a fellow student from home, someone with a name and a story, not a number.

passage:
Sunday night
Three months in Delhi now. At the college office, they call me "the outside one". "Tell the outside one to fill form B." In my part-time job at the courier office, the manager says "Hey, you," never Shankar. When a package went missing, he said, "Check with the new guys. Their kind loses things." I stood there like a chair. Something to move around.
I've started to feel like that inside too. Like I'm furniture. Last week I didn't call Amma because I didn't want to say how I felt.
But today Yusuf, from my maths class, waited for me after the lecture and said, "Shankar, come, my mother made biryani, she wants to meet you." Just my name, said properly. I sat in their kitchen for three hours. His mother asked about my village and my sister.
I called Amma tonight. I told her everything.

qa.q: What does the courier manager call Shankar?
qa.a: The manager says "Hey, you," never Shankar.

qa.q: How has being called "the outside one" affected how Shankar feels?
qa.a: Shankar feels hurt and empty, like furniture rather than a person, which even stopped the call to Amma.

qa.q: Why did the evening at Yusuf's house matter so much?
qa.a: Being called by name and asked about his village and sister reminded Shankar of being a person, and gave the strength to call Amma.

qa.q: How might Yusuf's mother see Shankar?
qa.a: She saw a student far from home worth meeting and feeding, someone with a village and a sister, not an outsider.

grounding: A migrant student's diary shows how being treated as a thing hurts deeply, and how a friend who uses Shankar's name helps reconnection.

During the wheat harvest in Moga, the polytechnic office was half-staffed, and the clerk never looked up. "Roll 117, form incomplete. You people always come late." Nitin had come from Darbhanga two months ago, and by now he answered to 117 faster than to his own name. In the workshop the instructor pointed at him with a spanner: "You, the outsider at the back." On the bus a man grumbled about "these fellows" taking all the seats.
That evening Nitin sat on the hostel roof, scrolling to his mother's number without calling.
Gurpreet climbed up with two glasses of lassi from the Baisakhi stall. "Nitin! You missed the bhangra. My chachi keeps asking where the boy who fixed her pump went."
Nitin laughed for the first time that day. He called his mother after that, and on Sunday he went to the fair in Gurpreet's village.

qa.q: What did the clerk call Nitin?
qa.a: "Roll 117", telling him the form was incomplete.

qa.q: What does Nitin scrolling to his mother's number without calling suggest?
qa.a: Nitin seems lonely and low, worn down by a day of being treated as a number and a burden, perhaps not wanting to worry his mother.

qa.q: What helped Nitin, and what else could help?
qa.a: Gurpreet using his name and pulling him into family and the fair helped; keeping close to people like his mother and Gurpreet, and raising the office's treatment with the hostel warden, could help more.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet see Nitin?
qa.a: To Gurpreet, Nitin is a person with a name and a place, the one who fixed the chachi's pump and was missed at the bhangra. 😊

grounding: A migrant student is called a roll number and an outsider, and staying close to someone who uses his name eases the pain.
